newsitem.title: USA: CIA nominee Lake to pay $5,000 fine on stock sales.
newsitem.headline: CIA nominee Lake to pay $5,000 fine on stock sales.

text.p: The Justice Department on Friday reached a civil settlement with former White House National Security Adviser Anthony Lake on his stock dealings and cleared him of lying to Congress about Bosnia arms policy.

Lake, nominated by President Bill Clinton to head the Central Intelligence Agency, agreed to pay a $5,000 civil penalty to settle allegations he violated conflict-of-interest laws by failing to sell four energy stocks after joining the White House in 1993.
A Justice Department spokesman said the civil settlement concluded the criminal investigation by its public integrity unit into the stock sales.

On the Bosnia arms policy, the Justice Department said it determined there was no basis for any criminal charges against Lake over allegations by House Republicans that he lied to Congress about the shipment of Iranian arms to Bosnia.
The Justice Department action cleared the way for the Senate Intelligence Committee to hold hearings late in February on Lake's nomination to be the top U.S. spymaster.

"The president is obviously delighted that the Justice Department has reached this agreement," White House spokesman Mike McCurry said. "The president fully expects that this information will now lay to rest any concerns that the Senate might have."
Clinton's choices of Lake and of former White House aide Alexis Herman as labour secretary have been the most controversial of the Cabinet nominations he has sent to the Republican-controlled Senate.

House Republicans in November asked the Justice Department to investigate whether Lake and other U.S. officials lied to Congress last September about the controversial policy to turn a blind eye to the flow of Iranian weapons to Bosnia Moslems in 1994, despite a U.N. arms embargo.

In a letter to the Republicans, Acting Assistant Attorney General Mark Richard said the Justice Department found "no direct, material contradictions between Mr. Lake's statements and the statements or testimony of other witnesses."
He said there was no evidence that Lake lied to the committee or was part of a conspiracy to obstruct Congress.
Lake has acknowleged making a mistake in not informing Congress of the Bosnia arms policy, but has denied any wrongdoing.
On the stock dealings, Lake was told after taking up his White House job that he must sell his personal holdings in Exxon Corp., Mobil Corp., Teco Energy Inc. and Duke Power Co.

The Justice Department said Lake thought his secretary had passed along his sell instructions to his broker and that the stocks had been sold. White House lawyers discovered in 1995 that he still owned the stocks. Lake then sold them.
Department lawyers said Lake from 1993 until 1995 received a number of documents, including routine statements from his broker, that he still owned the stocks.
They said Lake admitted that during that time he took part in several unspecified issues that "may have had a direct and predictable effect" on the two oil companies.

The lawyers said Lake acknowledged he took part in "a particular matter concerning negotiations with a foreign country, and Exxon Corp. was a potential beneficiary of a decision regarding that issue."

Under the settlement agreement, the Justice Derpartment maintained that Lake's conduct violated the law by his participation in a matter in which he had a financial interest. Lake denied the government's claim.
